source.title: SOAP, Muon, and Beyond: Pushing LLM Pretraining Scales
source.authors: Mikail Khona; Aditya Vavre; Bo-Xiang Wang; Deyu Fu; Hao Wu; Mike Chrzanowski; B. Catanzaro; Dheevatsa Mudigere; Jeff Pool; M. Lightstone; M. Shoeybi; M. Patwary; Nima Tajbakhsh; Tijmen Blankevoort

record.file_problem: The supplied full text is present. Some table values are flattened and cannot be reliably assigned to individual model and batch conditions.
record.tranche_reason: Tests batch-size effects on large language-model pretraining, extending the large-batch generalization question to MoE and hybrid LLMs.
record.gate_note: The study reports batch-size and optimizer comparisons using training loss, validation loss, and downstream evaluations. It does not test random-label memorization, width scaling, image CNN versus fully connected networks, dropout, sharpness measures, or memorized-example removal. Referenced results from other studies are not extracted.
record.test_reason: The fixed-token-horizon downstream evaluations test V5 in large-scale language-model pretraining. Equal token exposure provides the relevant budget comparison despite the absence of epoch terminology. Training-loss comparisons alone do not establish held-out performance.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the authors' conclusion: their modified SOAP and Muon outperform AdamW at the tested scales, and they recommend KL-SOAP when memory permits. This is their overall conclusion; Table 5 does not show uniform downstream improvement with increasing batch size.
record.recipe_differences: Large-scale LLM pretraining with MoE and hybrid models, token-based batch sizes, and training-loss/downstream evaluation rather than the image-classification and fixed-epoch comparisons described in V5.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size, optimizer, and batch-size ramp-up affect outcomes. The text also reports architectural sensitivity for applying Muon to Mamba Conv1D weights, but that result does not measure a V5 version claim.

fits_no_version.finding: Muon and modified SOAP show better large-batch training-loss convergence and stability than AdamW.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Large-batch optimization efficiency and stability depend on optimizer and preconditioner implementation.

record.problems: Some table values are flattened and cannot be assigned reliably. Several comparisons are shown only in figures. The paper reports training loss and downstream evaluations, not a direct train-test error gap; it states that training loss correlates with held-out validation loss on its dataset.
record.rows_left_out: Other batch-size and optimizer results are discussed in figures, but are not extracted where the text does not state a result or the figure provides no recoverable value. Table 7 compares precision formats and Lion, not a claim version.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum SGD; neither comparator is evaluated.

Image classification; longer-training remedies; isolated effects of normalization or regularization; held-out AdamW batch scaling; batch thresholds beyond the tested sizes. Optimizer changes and ramp-up are not independently isolated.
Dropout and its interactions with training-set size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware weight sharpness and its correlation with generalization gaps.
Removing memorized examples versus random examples.

record.verdict_notes: No original-source exclusion applies. Table 5's category averages are recoverable despite the flattened layout. Its mixed results should replace the record's blanket large-batch improvement interpretation. No uncertainty estimates establish whether small benchmark differences are statistically reliable.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum SGD on held-out performance under limited tuning; Muon comparisons do not test this stated contrast.
Fixed-epoch comparison; image-classification models; whether longer training, warmup, normalization, or regularization changes close the gap under matched budgets.
Dropout effects and its interaction with data augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to train-test gaps.
Removal of memorized training examples and resulting test accuracy.

rows.subject: NVIDIA-Nemotron-Nano-V3-30B-A3B
rows.operation_detail: Compared Muon at larger batch sizes with the AdamW baseline; figure reports loss trajectories.
rows.measure: Training loss and relative loss gaps against AdamW baseline
rows.note: The text says larger batches typically underperform and eventually exceed lower batch sizes as token horizon scales; the plot compares Muon 2x/3x with the AdamW baseline.
rows.check: Figure 1 measures training loss, not held-out performance. The stated correlation with validation loss does not supply validation results for these conditions. Comparisons against AdamW also change optimizer alongside batch size.

rows.subject: Hybrid Mamba-MoE 72B-A8B
rows.operation_detail: Compared Muon at 2x batch with the AdamW baseline, with a batch-size ramp-up.

conditions.value: Muon 2x the AdamW baseline batch size of 25M tokens

rows.measure: Training loss and downstream evaluation metrics
rows.value: Text reports lower loss and no loss spikes for Muon at larger batch; downstream results are reported in Table 5 but flattened
rows.note: The authors say Muon at the larger batch has lower loss and no loss spikes relative to the smaller-batch AdamW baseline.
rows.check: Split training loss, stability, and individual downstream metrics into separate rows. Only downstream results bear directly on V5. Muon at 50M tokens per batch outperforms AdamW at 25M on the reported category averages, but changing optimizer and batch schedule together prevents identifying a batch-size penalty. This comparison does bear on the adapted-recipe qualification.

source_check.correct: Split the measures. Training loss and loss spikes: cannot_determine for V5. Downstream results are mixed: Muon 2x versus AdamW 1x gives coding averages 63.48 versus 58.97, math averages 80.79 versus 84.04, and commonsense averages 83.31 versus 82.66. An aggregate downstream state is partial. Optimizer and batch size change together.
source_check.locator_found: Section 5.3; Figure 2 caption, p. 10; Table 5, p. 12.
source_check.problem: cannot_determine fits the training-loss and stability measures but does not describe the included, recoverable downstream results.

rows.subject: NVIDIA-Nemotron-Nano-V3 and 8B Hybrid MTP
rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream evaluation across Muon batch sizes and AdamW 1x batch.
rows.value: Table 5 reports benchmark results; individual values cannot be reliably assigned from the flattened layout
rows.note: The prose states Muon consistently matches or outperforms AdamW at baseline batch size and continues to improve as batch size scales, whereas AdamW does not; gains are most pronounced in coding and commonsense reasoning.
rows.check: Split by architecture, batch size, and benchmark. The second architecture has 72B total and 8B active parameters, rather than 8B total. Table 5 contains recoverable category averages and mixed within-Muon results: Nano math averages decline from 82.52 at 1x to 81.57 at 2x and 81.47 at 3x; coding averages change from 62.23 to 63.70 and 61.89. The prose claim of continued improvement is not uniform across metrics. Use Muon 1x as the baseline for within-optimizer batch comparisons.

source_check.correct: The second architecture has 72B total and 8B active parameters. Table 5 contains recoverable category averages. Nano-V3 Muon 1x/2x/3x: coding 62.23/63.70/61.89; math 82.52/81.57/81.47; MMLU 73.71/74.80/74.00; MMLU PRO CoT 58.19/56.77/55.61. The hybrid MTP comparison contains Muon 2x and AdamW 1x only.
source_check.locator_found: Section 5.3, architecture description immediately before Figure 3; Table 5, p. 12.
source_check.problem: The parameter description omits the second model's 72B total parameters, and the blanket claim that benchmark values cannot be assigned is incorrect.

rows.subject: NVIDIA-Nemotron-NanoV3
rows.operation_detail: Compared AdamW at 25M and 50M batch sizes with batch-size ramp-up and square-root scaling applied to the 50M run.

conditions.value: ramp-up and square-root scaling applied to 50M run

rows.note: The appendix states that techniques enabling larger-batch Muon pretraining did not help AdamW; the figure supplies the comparison without a textual result description.
rows.check: The baseline is AdamW at 25M tokens per batch. Figure 10 and Appendix C report training-loss behavior without corresponding held-out results. They cannot establish V5's held-out penalty.
